item.title: Japan's penalty hero wants more home fans to embrace women's game
item.description: Japan's penalty hero Yuzuho Shiokoshi hopes her team's soccer gold medal on home soil can get more local fans to embrace the women's game after a modest crowd attended their Asian Games shootout win over North Korea.
item.dc:creator: Ian Ransom
item.content:encoded: Japan's penalty hero Yuzuho Shiokoshi hopes her team's soccer gold medal on home soil can get more local fans to embrace the women's game after a modest crowd attended their Asian Games shootout win over North Korea. Some 6,000 people watched [USN:L6N45O0LF TEXT:"Friday's final"] at the 50,000-seat Shizuoka Stadium, while the host broadcaster opted to cover the men's volleyball semi-final between Japan and China instead. A day earlier, 65,000 spectators watched the Japanese men's national team beat Ecuador on penalties in the Kirin Cup in Yokohama. Japan's women claimed their third successive Asian Games gold, three years after beating North Korea in front of 37,000 fans in Hangzhou, China. "The crowd today might have been large for this tournament, but compared to last time in Hangzhou, I feel like we're still not quite there," said Shiokoshi, who struck the winning penalty on Friday. "We're out there fighting hard, and we want people to come and see us play in person. "It's tough at times, given that women's football isn't always prioritised for TV broadcasts." Japan selected a squad made up almost exclusively of home-based players rather than their top players in Europe despite the Games' tournament falling largely within the September-October international window. Shiokoshi, a midfielder for Tokyo Verdy Beleza in Japan's WE League, said her teammates' performances had been a good advertisement for the women's top flight. "I hope this encourages more people to come and watch WE League matches, and that it helps generate some excitement around the league," she said. “I think winning the title can boost the league’s value."

item.title: Bridge across Dnipro river in Kyiv hit during Russian attack, mayor says
item.description: The Northern Bridge across the Dnipro river in Kyiv was hit during a Russian air attack on Saturday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, amid an escalation in strikes on infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: The Northern Bridge across the Dnipro river in Kyiv was hit during a Russian air attack on Saturday, Mayor Vitali Klitschko said, amid an escalation in strikes on infrastructure in the Ukrainian capital. Emergency services were deployed to the scene, the mayor said, and traffic across the bridge from the east to the west bank was suspended following damage to the road surface and the overhead trolleybus cables. There were no casualties reported. In the past two days, the Southern Bridge has been struck several times by Russian drones, forcing the temporary suspension of traffic across it and two other bridges across the vast Dnipro river. Over a third of the capital's 3 million residents lived on the east, or "left", bank of the Dnipro before Russia's 2022 invasion, but the vast majority work on the western, or "right", bank where most government institutions and companies are. Memories of last winter, the worst of the war, are prominent in residents' minds after Russia launched last week what was seen in Ukraine as the first salvo of an expected winter bombing campaign against power facilities supplying the capital. Moscow has previously denied systematically targeting civilians as part of its bombing campaigns.

item.title: Swarms of moths in Australia lift hopes of recovery for endangered species
item.description: Swarms of moths blanketing homes in Australia's southeast in recent days signalled the endangered species is recovering, authorities said on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Reuters
item.content:encoded: Swarms of moths blanketing homes in Australia's southeast in recent days signalled the endangered species is recovering, authorities said on Saturday. Bogong moths, with a wingspan of up to 5 cm (2 inches), have experienced years of steep population decline, decreasing the visibility of their southern spring migration to caves in the Australian Alps in a journey that can be up to 3,000 km (1,900 miles). But the moths have had a comeback this year, with reports that the insects have invaded backyards and homes along Australia's east coast, including in New South Wales state capital, Sydney. "It’s really exciting to see this recovering population coming our way," Steve Whan, who represents the alpine area of Monaro in the New South Wales parliament, said in a statement. "The Bogongs are terrific for our ecosystem, supporting our treasured native wildlife like the pygmy-possum and pollinating our eucalyptus trees." In neighbouring Victoria state, Chief Biodiversity Officer James Todd said it was exciting to see the moths returning in large numbers this year. "The jump in numbers is a positive sign for biodiversity," Todd said in a statement. The numbers of the moths, which are harmless to humans and legally protected, have fallen due to drought, agricultural intensification and habitat loss, authorities say. One theory for the rebound is more rainfall in northern New South Wales producing extra food for the insects' larvae, the Australian Broadcasting Corp reported.

item.title: Canucks eager to fix defensive problems as Flames visit
item.description: The Vancouver Canucks will try to shore up a leaky defense when they host the Calgary Flames on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The Vancouver Canucks will try to shore up a leaky defense when they host the Calgary Flames on Saturday. Vancouver finished with the lowest point total in the NHL last season (58) while permitting a league-leading 314 goals. The early returns on the new season show no improvement in the latter area. The Canucks surrendered 14 goals in a home-and-home series against the Oilers. Vancouver won the season opener 6-5 in overtime at Edmonton. Two nights later in Vancouver, the Oilers jumped out to a 5-0 lead early in the second period and then held on for a 9-7 victory. "That wasn't anywhere near close to good enough," said Canucks defenseman Luke Schenn, one of the veterans the team brought in during the offseason to bring leadership to the dressing room. "(The Oilers) got a couple of guys that are elite players. You give them a ton of respect and they are going to burn you." Schenn warned his teammates against getting selfish with the puck. "You get on your own program at times," he said. "You become an individual and turn the puck over, get sloppy and hang your goalie out to dry on breakaways. The good news on both sides is we don't have to see (Edmonton) for awhile." First-year coach Manny Malhotra wasn't happy with the way Vancouver fell behind 8-2 halfway through the Thursday game after giving up short-handed goals to Connor McDavid and Kasperi Kapanen 34 seconds apart on the same penalty kill. "We didn't seem to be as prepared as we needed to be," Malhotra said. "That is how the game got away from us. We lost the majority of puck battles and the majority of races. They were more hungrier." The Canucks are firmly in rebuild mode. Last season was a dismal campaign for Vancouver, punctuated by a franchise-record 11-game losing streak (0-9-2) and the departure of captain Quinn Hughes, who soured on playing in Vancouver and was traded to the Minnesota Wild in December. Vancouver is still without a captain. Instead of giving the "C" to someone else, the Canucks decided to appoint six alternate captains. The Flames are also trying to get over a poor 2025-26 season, when they tied for the NHL's third-lowest point total (77). The biggest problem was an offense that produced a league-low 208 goals. Calgary was hammered 6-1 in its season opener by the visiting Seattle Kraken on Thursday, the Flames' largest margin of defeat ever in a home opener. Ryan Strome scored for the Flames. Goalie Dustin Wolf stopped 26 shots against Seattle in what is expected to be the final season opener at the Saddledome. "You saw all our warts in one night," coach Ryan Huska said. Like the Canucks, the Flames fell behind early and gave up five consecutive goals to start the game. Calgary was outshot 32-25 and had just one power play while conceding five. "That one stings," Strome said. "It is disappointing. We are a team that can't make any mistakes. We got to play hard and we got to play simple. Getting away from that was what you saw tonight." --Field Level Media

item.title: Sharks push for more early-season success against Kings
item.description: The San Jose Sharks will look to show more of their identity when they face the visiting Los Angeles Kings on Saturday.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: The San Jose Sharks will look to show more of their identity when they face the visiting Los Angeles Kings on Saturday. San Jose opened the season with a 4-3 overtime win over the Florida Panthers on Thursday. Will Smith scored two goals and added an assist, and Mason Marchment also tallied in his Sharks debut as San Jose opened a 3-0 lead. Luca Cagnoni added his first career goal in the extra period after the Sharks squandered the lead in regulation. Macklin Celebrini contributed three assists and Yaroslav Askarov made 23 saves in the win. "There was a lot going on in that game, a lot that we can kind of build off of and learn from," Sharks coach Ryan Warsofsky said. "We said it before the game: It wasn't going to be perfect, we weren't going to be perfect. But we wanted to show our identity, and I thought we did that more often (on Thursday) than we probably have in the last couple years." Saturday is the first of four meetings between the Pacific Division rivals. San Jose won two of three matchups with the Kings last season. Askarov, the Sharks' expected starter, is 3-1-0 with a 2.94 goals-against average and an .878 save percentage in four career appearances against the Kings. Following the Saturday contest, the Sharks head on the road for a pair of Central Division matchups against the Dallas Stars on Monday and the St. Louis Blues on Thursday. "We want to play fast, we want to get on teams with our team speed, but we need to be physical, and that's what winning teams do. They're physical all over the ice," Warsofsky said. "That doesn't mean you're running around trying to put people into Section 220 in the stands. It's just playing through people and being hard to play against." The Kings travel to San Jose cap a two-game, season-opening road trip after being doubled up 8-4 by the Colorado Avalanche in Denver on Wednesday. Brian Dumoulin, Joel Armia, Trevor Moore and Artemi Panarin scored for the Kings. Alex Laferriere added two assists in Los Angeles' first regular-season game under new coach Peter Laviolette. Darcy Kuemper made 21 saves in the loss. "I think that there were things that we did well and I think that there are things that we need to clean up and do better," Laviolette said. "I felt like a lot of the things that we gave (Colorado) were our responsibility. They are things that can be in our control: staying out of the penalty box, the execution of what we're doing, staying behind the rush. We got chances to score offensively, and we didn't connect on them. "So we found ourselves chasing the game most of the night." In 22 career games against the Sharks, Kuemper is 10-5-5 with a .909 save percentage and a 2.78 GAA. The Kings head back to Los Angeles following the Saturday game for their home opener against the Panthers on Tuesday. --Field Level Media

item.title: Leo Carlsson, Ducks start strong, hold off Golden Knights’ surge
item.description: Leo Carlsson had a goal and an assist and Lukas Dostal made 27 saves as the Anaheim Ducks jumped out to a big early lead and held on for a 4-3 victory over the Vegas Golden Knights on Friday night in Las Vegas.
item.dc:creator: Field Level Media
item.content:encoded: Leo Carlsson had a goal and an assist and Lukas Dostal made 27 saves as the Anaheim Ducks jumped out to a big early lead and held on for a 4-3 victory over the Vegas Golden Knights on Friday night in Las Vegas. Beckett Sennecke, Alex Killorn and Jeff Malott also scored goals for Anaheim in its season-opener. Shea Theodore, Tomas Hertl and Braeden Bowman scored goals and Jack Eichel had two assists for Vegas, which lost in regulation for just the fourth time (15-4-1) in 20 regular-season games against Anaheim at T-Mobile Arena. Carter Hart finished with 16 saves for the Golden Knights. Anaheim took a 1-0 lead at the 19:52 mark of the first period on a breakaway goal by Sennecke. Carlsson picked up the primary assist on the play with a highlight-reel stretch pass from deep in his own zone to Sennecke, who snuck behind a pair of Vegas defenders and then beat Hart with a wrist shot on his glove side. The Ducks extended the lead to 4-0 in the second period, scoring twice in the span of 55 seconds early in the period. Killorn, stationed in the slot, made it 2-0 at the 1:33 mark when he redirected Noah Warren's wrist shot from the right point over Hart's right shoulder. Warren, making his NHL debut, picked up an assist for his first career point. Malott followed with a goal on a double deflection. Jackson LaCombe fired a shot from the left point that Tim Washe deflected off Malott's skate and under Hart's pads. A wide-open Carlsson made it a four-goal lead at the 7:03 mark when he slammed in a rebound in the slot after Hart had turned away shots by Cutter Gauthier and A.J. Greer. Theodore cut the lead to 4-1 early in the third period when he snapped a wrist shot from the middle of the right circle over Dostal's left shoulder. Anaheim unsuccessfully challenged that Brett Howden was offside earlier in the play, earning the Ducks a two-minute delay of game penalty when the goal stood. Hertl then scored on the ensuing power play with a wrist shot in the slot off a Mitch Marner pass. Bowman then cut the deficit to one goal when he put in a rebound of a Victor Olofsson shot with 2:50 to go to make it 4-3. Vegas pulled Hart for an extra attacker with 2:15 left but Dostal turned away three shots in that final stretch. --Field Level Media

item.title: AI's race to transform the world before the money runs out
item.description: Never has so much cash flowed into a new technology as is pouring into AI, eclipsing the sums splurged on railways or the internet when those technological revolutions sucked in capital.
item.dc:creator: Stephen Eisenhammer
item.content:encoded: Never has so much cash flowed into a new technology as is pouring into AI, eclipsing the sums splurged on railways or the internet when those technological revolutions sucked in capital. Cumulative spending globally on data centers alone could top $30 trillion by 2050, according to a projection by PwC, almost matching the [USN:S0N43F052 TEXT:"value of outstanding US Treasuries"]. It "dwarfs" what was spent in the railroad or dotcom booms, even after adjusting for inflation, PwC said. Meanwhile, Anthropic, just one of the major firms in the AI race, plans to spend $518 billion in coming years, according to the [USN:L4N4500J8 TEXT:"IPO prospectus seen by Reuters"], which is more than 100 times its 2025 revenue. Its backers say AI technology will be more transformational than the advent of steam engines and the industrialization they powered. Yet lurking behind the dizzying projections and huge outlays by AI companies, alongside sky-high valuations, lie assumptions about vast broad-based productivity gains and future profits with little evidence so far - or historical precedent - to be sure they can deliver, economists say. PRODUCTIVITY GAINS 'REMAIN ELUSIVE' JP Morgan wrote in August that broad-based productivity gains in the US, which leads the AI race, "remain elusive", raising questions about the sustainability of AI valuations. A Bain & Company study said productivity gains from existing markets would not be enough to justify current outlays and "entirely new markets must emerge to close the funding gap", suggesting those could range from using AI-guided robots to developing new materials for batteries and semiconductors. US hyperscalers - the companies rolling out infrastructure around the world like Google, Amazon and Microsoft - and others in the AI race needed to find more than $4.2 trillion of new revenue in the next five years to fund the buildout, Bain said. "The question is whether the applications arrive in time to pay for it," according to the study, published last month. Few doubt the potential of AI to transform everything from work in an office to research labs, just as past revolutions shrank journey times from days to hours or connected the world at the touch of a keyboard. What seems more immutable is the maths behind securing a return on investment or the deadlines for repaying loans, leaving economists to work out the implications for the global economy beyond the ups and downs of investment cycles. "Historical precedent suggests that technology-driven booms often end when infrastructure buildouts cease to deliver sufficient returns," JP Morgan wrote. Using the example of Nvidia, the US company [USN:L1N45L0J4 TEXT:"whose chips are the backbone"] of the AI revolution, JP Morgan estimated US productivity gains would need to be 3% to 5% annually over the next 10 years to justify its valuation. That would be a substantial increase from the baseline expectation of the US Congressional Budget Office of 1.75% annual productivity growth for that period. For the US alone - which according to some estimates accounts for about three quarters of the global AI investment total - investment will run as high as about $9 trillion from 2025 to 2032, equivalent to spending 3.2% of US GDP each year, according to Columbia Business School economist Stijn Van Nieuwerburgh. He estimates the US AI sector would need to generate about $3.55 trillion in annual revenue by 2032 to earn a 10% return on investment. It earns a fraction of that now. The leveraged structure of much of the debt funding AI infrastructure also means "a relatively modest deterioration in demand, delays, or asset values can therefore produce much larger losses," he wrote in a conference paper, revised in October. AI AND 'THE RATE OF NEW WONDERS' The dizzying numbers have not stopped US AI bosses speaking with an otherworldly zeal about changes afoot. Anthropic's Dario Amodei has said an AI future could be "a thing of transcendent beauty", while OpenAI's Sam Altman has said "the rate of new wonders being achieved will be immense" as models learn to improve themselves and accelerate breakthroughs. Jasjeet Sekhon, chief strategy officer at Google DeepMind, told a summit at UC Berkeley in August that this self-teaching, known as recursive self-improvement, was a "key part of the investment thesis", and that it could, if achieved, deliver unprecedented productivity gains. Recursive self-improvement, while potentially delivering exponential AI advances, has also raised concerns about [USN:L4N45K1J5 TEXT:"existential risks"] to humanity. Yet the pace of change in productivity might still end up lagging the timelines needed by corporate accounts departments. Diane Coyle, an economist at Britain's Cambridge University, said the productivity impact of past revolutionary technologies had usually taken about 10 to 50 years to feed through. Anthropic's economics team modeled a range of scenarios for how much extra growth AI would deliver at an annual rate in 2030. Assuming a baseline of 2% in a non-AI environment, it suggested growth of 2.4% in a scenario with modest AI impact, 5.4% in a substantial scenario and 15.4% in an extreme scenario. Higher growth would mean more jobs lost, it said, without assigning probabilities for any of the outcomes. Amodei forecast last year that AI could wipe out half of all entry-level white-collar jobs within five years. For now, however, some researchers say it appears to have been limited to making it harder for those seeking office work to find a job. Studies in the US and Britain have pointed to a slowdown in early career hiring for white-collar positions performing tasks at which AI is adept, even if overall employment remains strong. Researchers at Stanford University said in August that employment of workers aged 22 to 25 in AI-exposed industries, such as accountants and paralegals, was 19% lower than for jobs that AI found hard to replicate, like janitors and builders. Yet even if the promised transformation takes longer than numbers surrounding AI companies imply, real economic benefits should stay - just as trains still ran after the Panic of 1873 that bankrupted railroad barons, while the internet didn't shut down after the 1990s dotcom bubble burst. "History is our friend in trying to understand this," said Coyle. "As long as one is left with the infrastructure that's needed to support all the productivity effects down the road, that's okay."

item.title: When your journalism goes to Hollywood | On Assignment
item.description: Reporter Jeff Horwitz reflects on his Hollywood alter ego, and the reporting that landed on the big screen.
item.content:encoded: Follow on Apple or Spotify . Listen on the Reuters app. Reporter Jeff Horwitz is having a surreal week. His investigation into Facebook has been turned into a major Hollywood film starring Jeremy Allen White. On this episode of On Assignment , the Pulitzer Prize-winning Reuters journalist reflects on the Facebook Files investigation, his relationship with whistleblower Frances Haugen, and the impact the revelations had on the debate over social media's harms. He also shares what it's like to see his own story transformed for the big screen in Aaron Sorkin's The Social Reckoning .
